claims.text: The FeNiCrCoCu coating on a Cu matrix has high elastic modulus at 300 K.
The coating has stable wear resistance at 300 K.
The initial coating contains a pre-existing network of dislocations.
The initial coating contains pre-existing stacking faults.
Increasing temperature under nanoindentation and frictional loading thermally reduces the stacking-fault energy.
Increasing temperature changes deformation from localized dislocation glide to homogeneous lattice disordering.
Below a critical temperature, stable stacking faults impede dislocation motion.
The impediment of dislocation motion by stacking faults maintains wear resistance below the critical temperature.
Thermal energy promotes atomic mixing and disordering as temperature rises.
Thermally promoted atomic disorder causes a sharp drop in stacking-fault energy.
A sharp reduction in stacking-fault energy permits stacking faults to merge into amorphous-like regions.
Elevated temperature may enable rapid dislocation climb that bypasses defect-mediated hardening.
Thermally activated atomic disordering above a critical threshold overcomes the stabilizing effect of high dislocation density.
Bypassing defect-mediated hardening causes lattice softening.
Wear resistance declines sharply once temperature exceeds the critical threshold.
Elastic modulus declines sharply once temperature exceeds the critical threshold.
Crossing the critical threshold changes deformation from localized plasticity to rapid, catastrophic lattice disordering.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to alloys whose atomic-size mismatch or electronic structure stabilizes the lattice at higher temperatures.
